market.text: FACT//DUEL Product Market Decisions
Positioning and launch decision

Build a focused knowledge game around **“Pick your obsession. Challenge someone. Leave knowing more.”** The first product should serve people who enjoy proving specific knowledge to friends, with a satisfying explanation after the result. Sports history supplies identity and rivalry; science supplies curiosity and discovery. This is a product hypothesis, not evidence that the combined audience already wants the game.

The executive decision is to retain one recognizable duel interaction and make topic selection, readable answers, trustworthy results and rematches excellent. Launch research in three wedges: India cricket enthusiasts, European football supporters, and US-led space/science enthusiasts. Keep US basketball and American football available as expansion decks, but do not spread the initial acquisition experiment across every sport. The niche advantage must come from editorial depth and a coherent experience, not the number of menus.

Evidence was checked on **12 September 2026**. Competitor descriptions below come from current developer listings and official help pages; no private retention data or proprietary code was inspected. Market arithmetic is explicitly hypothetical. The current private prototype, its sample bank and bot sessions do not constitute demonstrated market demand.
Current product comparison

rows: Current positioning emphasizes The Floor episodes each Thursday, specialist champions, friend challenges and a dedicated leaderboard; ads and in-app purchases are declared. [Developer listing](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.etermax.preguntados.lite)
Expert identity, seasonal programming and friend competition already exist. Make the path into a chosen subject shorter and the fact reveal more useful.
Store installs are cumulative; rankings and reviews do not establish current active users, retention or dissatisfaction prevalence.

Developer advertises over two million quizzes, varied formats, daily puzzles, badges, streaks, missions, creation and playlists; Orange adds ad removal and other features. [Developer listing](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sporcle.geneva)
Topic depth and daily play are established expectations. A small verified bank should promise its actual coverage rather than compete on inventory size.
Public inventory does not establish consistent question quality or engagement per quiz.

Live hosting, self-paced challenges, flashcards, study leagues and quiz creation; premium features depend on user context. [Developer listing](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=no.mobitroll.kahoot.android)
Easy room entry and distinct competitive/practice experiences matter. Avoid making every user configure a classroom-style event.
The listing does not disclose timing arbitration, anti-cheat logic or customer unit economics.
**Blooket**, official help accessed 12 Sep 2026; publication date not shown
Over 25 modes, including live, solo and homework; Battle Royale explicitly supports 1v1 encounters. [Mode guide](https://help.blooket.com/hc/en-us/articles/21408591795351-Blooket-Game-Mode-Previews)
A large mode catalog is not a differentiator. Reuse a verified question model across a small set of genuinely different play objectives.
Mode count does not prove learning effectiveness, retention or demand for adult specialist duels.

Streaks, weekly leagues, Friends Quests and mutual Friend Streaks support repeated practice and social commitment. [Motivation features](https://blog.duolingo.com/sticking-with-it-tips-for-staying-motivated/), [Friend Streak](https://blog.duolingo.com/friend-streak/)
Make personal progress and consensual friend rituals visible. Experiment with a weekly knowledge goal and an explicit stopping point.
Company-reported associations between social features and completion do not establish causation or transferable trivia retention.

market.text: The combined opportunity is **specialist rivalry with an explanation worth keeping**. Each component has precedents. Whether the combination earns preference requires observed behavior against the alternatives. Do not claim novelty, market leadership or “scientifically addictive” design.

The home screen should offer a primary practice action, an equally clear friend-room action, and three editorial collections. Show the selected topic, mode and opponent type before starting. After a round, prioritize the outcome, correct answer and short explanation; place one rematch action nearby. Coins remain clearly fictional and secondary to knowledge. Avoid interrupting this loop with multiple reward dialogs. This is an executive design choice to validate, not a proven universal rule.
Audience evidence and its boundaries

rows: ITU estimates **6.0 billion people online, 74% of the population, in 2025**. [ITU statistics](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/pages/stat/default.aspx)
A broad online ceiling, not a trivia TAM.

ICC reports **72.5 million digital concurrent users** for the men's T20 World Cup final on 8 Mar 2026; published 23 Mar. [ICC](https://www.icc-cricket.com/media-releases/a-game-for-the-world-cricket-s-growth-horizons)
Supports an India cricket recruitment hypothesis. A streaming peak is neither unique annual fandom nor app demand.

UEFA's 27 Jul 2025 Women's EURO report anticipated **over 400 million cumulative live audience** and **over 45 million final viewers**. [UEFA](https://www.uefa.com/womenseuro/news/029b-1e522ecda3bd-ccdd22a6bb3c-1000--milestones-met-history-made-record-breaking-women-s-euro-rea/)
A historical projection and broad distribution signal; not final observed reach or an EU-only count. Include women's competitions within normal football coverage.

Nielsen revised Super Bowl LX to **125.6 million viewers**, published 19 Feb 2026 for the 8 Feb telecast. [Nielsen](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/nielsen-super-bowl-lx-final-viewership-rises-to-125-6-million-viewers-with-verified-big-data/)
US expansion evidence. Do not add this audience to other sports as distinct prospects.

Commission summary published 3 Feb 2025: **58% want to learn more** about scientific developments; lack of time is one reported barrier. [European Commission](https://cyprus.representation.ec.europa.eu/news/europeans-strongly-support-science-and-technology-according-new-eurobarometer-survey-2025-02-03_en)
Supports testing short science sessions; the question does not measure gaming interest.

Pew's 20 Jul 2023 report found **47% of US adults** had done at least one of four specified space-related activities in the previous year. [Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/07/20/americans-views-of-space-u-s-role-nasa-priorities-and-impact-of-private-companies/)
A defined but older entry-point signal. Occasional engagement is broader than enthusiast identity or competition demand.

market.text: These observations cannot be summed. They mix people, concurrent users, projected cumulative audiences and survey responses. No verified representative measure of India's science-trivia demand was found in this update. The football choice also relies on content suitability and reachable communities, not a numerical proof that football is the largest addressable segment. The earlier 2022 FIFA figures are deliberately not used in this model; this update did not recover a complete comparable newer global unique-audience report.
TAM, SAM and obtainable cohort

There is **no measured FACT//DUEL TAM or SAM yet**. The following user scenarios preserve the prior model for continuity and expose the assumptions that research must replace. They are not forecasts, confidence intervals, registrations or revenue estimates.

Define future global user TAM as online adults who would choose a free sports/science trivia product with sufficient languages and content. The formula is `6,000 million × 75% assumed adult share × joint product-interest rate`. Joint interest includes both subject interest and willingness to play this format; it avoids adding sports fans to science enthusiasts. Interest rates of 5%, 10% and 20% imply **225m, 450m and 900m** respectively. The generous language/content premise is a future possibility, not today's capability.

Define planning SAM as US, India, EU27 and UK residents who are online adults, comfortable reading the actual English cards, and interested in the product: `Σ population × online fraction × adult fraction among online users × English readiness × joint interest`. “Europe” means EU27 plus UK here; other European countries are excluded. No sport-fandom percentage is multiplied into the model.

rows: Adult share among online users, assumed

market.text: Population and available internet inputs were rechecked on World Bank country pages: [US](https://data.worldbank.org/country/united-states), [India](https://data.worldbank.org/country/india), [EU](https://data.worldbank.org/country/european-union), [UK](https://data.worldbank.org/country/united-kingdom). The EU page displayed no aggregate internet value. All adult shares, English readiness and product-interest rates are assumptions; conversational English surveys cannot establish rapid specialist reading ability.

Arithmetic precision is not measurement confidence. Halving base joint interest halves SAM to approximately **28.8m**. At base interest, reducing India English readiness from 18% to 10% lowers total SAM by approximately **6.1m**. A different reading-speed requirement could therefore change the reachable audience more than a visual theme. Appropriate device access, editorial coverage and actual product availability still limit serviceability. The private site's accessible cohort is much smaller than these future scenarios.

SOM should start from distribution actually secured. For an illustrative six-week recruitment effort, define retained pilot users as distinct eligible prospects reached through permitted communities × first-match completion × return in days 22–28. Deduplicate people belonging to several communities. Every value below is an assumed planning input; no communities or users have been secured by this research.

The product currently has no paid offering, so current transaction revenue is zero. A hypothetical dollar TAM would add unsupported payer and pricing assumptions. Consider ad-free presentation, cosmetic themes or creator hosting tools only after repeat play is demonstrated. Do not finance the experience through paid answer advantages or inflated fictional balances.
Three acquisition wedges

rows: India ODI/T20 history, completed World Cups, IPL/WPL moments, players and venues; separate formats and eras
Test whether a friend-room invitation settles familiar debates and prompts voluntary rematches. Recruit through explicitly permitted adult fan and alumni groups.
Add Hindi or another requested language only after observing English reading friction and recruiting language reviewers.
World Cups, Euros, Champions League and selected club histories, including women's competitions
Test whether a recognizable club/era choice creates stronger preference than random broad trivia. Recruit permitted supporter groups; avoid implying club endorsement.
Expand club filters only when each advertised deck has enough reviewed facts to prevent immediate repetition.
Solar system, missions, light, motion and surprising life-science basics; optional deeper branches
Test whether a satisfying explanation creates repeat visits even after losing. Recruit consenting astronomy, maker and science-education communities.
Add chemistry, computing, awards and advanced physics according to observed choice and source coverage; test US basketball/NFL collections separately.

market.text: Use the same visual system across wedges, with editorial imagery and accent changes that preserve predictable answer colors and controls. Test one meaningful proposition per recruitment page. A combined sports-science crossover collection can explore ball flight, friction, reaction time and materials, but should earn its place through play data.

Practice bots solve the empty-room experience, not multiplayer liquidity. Label random guessing and randomized response timing honestly; do not present a random bot as a calibrated expert. Track bot play separately from human invitations, accepted challenges and completed human matches. Keep topic choice broad enough for discovery while avoiding dozens of empty public queues.
Decision gates and progress tracking

The thresholds below are **management hypotheses**, not industry benchmarks. Start with moderated sessions, then recruit at least 100 activated participants per wedge across multiple communities before deciding where to invest. Report uncertainty and recruitment bias; small differences are not proof of a winning segment.

rows: Observe first practice match; ask player to explain timer, wrong answers and bot identity
At least 8/10 moderated participants complete without assistance and explain the basic rule
Repeated confusion: simplify setup before adding modes
Completed first match / eligible unique starters
At least 70% in each pilot wedge
Below 50% after one repair cycle: investigate loading, reading and setup friction
Return in days 7–13; bot and human cohorts separate
At least 25% of activated players return, with qualitative reasons consistent with the proposition
Below 15% after two content/flow iterations: pause expansion
Voluntary friend invitations and accepted-room completion
At least 15% invite; at least 50% of accepted invitations become completed matches
High sharing but failed matches: repair access/room flow before acquisition
Verified answer errors; disputes per 100 completed rounds; explained timing outcomes
No known critical factual errors remain; at least 90% in a comprehension sample can interpret results
Unexplained outcomes, misleading bot identity or unresolved critical errors block cohort growth
Review throughput, correction age, unseen-question coverage
Each promoted narrow deck has at least 40 reviewed fact families and an assigned maintainer
Repetition or unreviewed automated material: reduce advertised scope

market.text: Instrument consented events for setup start, topic choice, match start/completion, opponent type, invitation acceptance, rematch, explanation opening and question dispute. Count people, matches and rounds separately. Do not manufacture online-player counts, global rankings, measured mastery or cohort retention from local storage, bot sessions or internal tests.

For progress tracking, each roadmap issue needs one accountable owner, hypothesis, dependency, acceptance evidence, status and decision date. The next investment decision should follow real completion, trust and return behavior. TAM remains context; the experiment is whether a small group voluntarily chooses a second and third session.

design.text: FACT DUEL Game and Experience Design
Product decision

Build a welcoming knowledge arena around **“Know your world. Play your people.”** The distinctive promise is a short challenge about something a person already cares about, followed by a fact worth keeping. Topic identity, understandable rules, trustworthy explanations, and easy repeat play should carry the experience. Demo coins provide optional match stakes; they should not dominate the navigation, resemble a cash balance, or imply that buying an advantage is possible.

For the first product release, concentrate the interaction model into three destinations: **Play**, **Explore**, and **Notebook**. Play contains the existing Quick Draw and Triple Threat, with a clearly labelled practice bot as the quickest entry and private friend rooms as the social path. Explore selects a field and a precise question pool. Notebook is proposed personal review, initially stored on this device with that limitation visible. An untimed solo practice path is a launch priority; it is a separate experience, not a claim that a reflex race measures knowledge equally for everyone.

This is a recommendation for the private, free-coin product. The existing 150 ms draw band and browser-reported local duration are casual fairness rules, not proof of physical simultaneity or cheat resistance. A random bot has a 25% chance of choosing the correct option only when all four choices are sampled uniformly. Its choice and delay must remain independent of the human response, and it must never appear as a real person.
Evidence translated into design

Ryan, Rigby, and Przybylski’s four studies linked perceived autonomy, competence, and, in multiplayer settings, relatedness with enjoyment and future play. The authors also identified limits in sampled genres, assigned laboratory play, and measurement generalizability. Use this as a design hypothesis: offer meaningful topic choice, legible feedback, and voluntary social play. It does not establish a retention uplift for trivia. Avoid describing a cosmetic badge as psychological need satisfaction. [1](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2006_RyanRigbyPrzybylski_MandE.pdf)

Roediger and Karpicke found benefits of retrieval over restudy on delayed tests of studied prose; their experiments used free recall rather than this timed four-choice game. Butler and Roediger more directly examined multiple-choice testing: feedback increased later correct recall and reduced intrusion of wrong alternatives compared with no feedback. The product inference is to show the correct answer and an original explanation after settlement, then offer later retrieval. Faster tapping is not evidence of durable learning. [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16507066/) [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18491500/)

The book material inspected is limited to accessible author excerpts, descriptions, and tables of contents. Norman’s author page emphasizes signifiers, feedback, conceptual models, and designing for error. Krug’s publisher overview and contents emphasize intuitive navigation, concise copy, mobile usability, and inexpensive usability testing. Translate those ideas into plainly named controls, one main action per state, visible pending/accepted distinctions, and recovery that preserves selections. No complete book-reading claim is warranted. [4](https://jnd.org/books/the-design-of-everyday-things-revised-and-expanded-edition/) [5](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/don-t-make-me-think-revisited-a-common-sense-approach-to-web-usability/P200000000385/9780133597264)

Schell’s publisher description recommends examining a game through many perspectives and iterating; use a player, rules, aesthetics, and fairness review for every feature. Koster’s published first-chapter excerpt describes disengagement when a challenge is too difficult, too easy, or exhausted. These are useful practitioner lenses, not validated difficulty thresholds. Keep variety in question families and let people choose challenge depth; do not silently alter the competitive question to engineer a win. [6](https://www.routledge.com/about-us/crc-press) [7](https://www.theoryoffun.com/excerpt.shtml)
Artistic direction and color

Use an editorial sports almanac crossed with a modern science journal: oversized numerals, confident typography, generous breathing room, small diagram-like topic illustrations, and a restrained arena motif. A persistent cyan-versus-magenta split would overemphasize competition; use player initials and explicit labels instead. Avoid unlicensed team crests or photos as identity shortcuts. The visual direction is an original creative decision rather than a neuroscience claim.

rows: Topic illustration and labelled category accent
Topic illustration and labelled category accent
Error icon and explanatory text, never color alone

design.text: Calculated opaque sRGB contrast is 14.35:1 for ink on ivory, 12.78:1 for ink on lime, and 15.82:1 for pale text on arena green. Blue, amber, and coral against arena green calculate to 10.05:1, 10.99:1, and 7.89:1 respectively. These checks cover these pairs only; actual rendered hover, disabled, translucent, and light-theme variants still need verification. Dark text on blue or amber chips is preferable to pale text.

A 4,598-person, 30-nation color-association study found shared patterns with linguistic and geographical variation. It measured associations with color terms, not this interface’s conversion, trust, or reaction speed. Therefore, do not promise that a hue makes users calmer, smarter, or more likely to pay. Test recognition, readability, and preference across target cohorts. [8](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797620948810)
Screen-by-screen contract

rows: A compact promise, remembered topic, two mode cards, visible bot/friend selection. Avoid a long carousel before play.
Primary “Play a practice bot”; secondary “Challenge a friend.” Clearly state free coins and bot randomness.
Start with Sports / Science; then field, competition or concept, entity/era, and depth. Show breadcrumb, exact available count, and sample scope.
Empty pools explain what is missing; offer an explicit broader filter rather than silently broadening.
Show mode length, timer, single-attempt rule, optional coin stake, and close-answer policy in a compact summary.
One “Create match” action. Keep advanced timing explanation behind a labelled disclosure.
Two seat cards, initials, human/bot badge, actual readiness, room code and copy action. Do not fabricate searching players or queue activity.
“I’m ready”; copy confirmation as text. Explain a room invite does not bypass private site access.
Stable question region and answer placeholders; large countdown without zooming or flashing.
A visible start cue. A pre-round cancel remains distinct from an active-round exit.
Question above four full-width answers on small phones; 2×2 answers only when labels fit comfortably. Fixed option order during the round.
“One answer. Tap to lock.” Timer is readable but visually secondary to the question.
Immediately mark the chosen option and prevent a second choice. Keep the same question visible.
“Sending your answer…” is distinct from “Answer received.” Retry the immutable attempt automatically where safe.
Retain the selected answer and calm status; do not reveal an opponent’s choice, correctness, or answer event prematurely.
“Comparing answers…”; explain delay if necessary without asserting an unconfirmed result.
Outcome, each player’s correctness and reported duration, draw explanation when relevant, coin settlement, then the sourced explanation.
“Next round” or “Play again,” alongside “Save fact” and “Finish.” No automatic rematch countdown.
Saved facts with topic, source, date, and optional later four-choice review. Label local storage and offer clear/delete controls.
“Review 3 facts” is a bounded session. Never equate saved or seen facts with mastery.
Light/dark/system, sound, motion preference, shortcut guidance, and input/accessibility information.
Show sound preview only after an explicit action. Preserve choices without mandatory registration.
Specific room full, expired invite, offline, or session-cancelled message, with any refund status taken from confirmed state.
Preserve setup where possible; use “Retry,” “Return to room,” or “Create another room,” rather than one generic error.

design.text: These are screen contracts, not a statement that every destination is implemented. The roadmap should track each capability separately from its visual mockup.
Sound, motion, and input

Brewster, Wright, and Edwards’ research-based earcon guidance recommends recognizably different rhythm and timbre, short cues, and controlled intensity; pitch alone can be a poor identifier. Their work concerns interface communication, not evidence that an audio flourish improves trivia retention. Use a tiny original synthesized family and test it on phone speakers. All cues remain optional and duplicate visible information. [9](https://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/~stephen/earcon_guidelines.shtml)

rows: One soft wooden click, around 80–120 ms
Two short, distinct plucked notes, around 220 ms total
No timing depends on audio playback
Server acceptance cue; pending state stays visually distinct
Gentle low double pulse, around 200 ms
No buzzer, insult, or volume jump

design.text: Keep sound off initially, provide an always-reachable mute, and suppress cues on hidden tabs. No background music, accelerating final-second ticks, coin-machine cascades, or flashing confetti in the initial release. Reduced motion replaces ornamental movement with instant state changes; do not remove information with the animation. These durations and timbres are design proposals requiring listening tests, not validated thresholds.

Set answer pads to at least 56 CSS px high where content permits, with wrapping and 8–12 px separation; ordinary controls should target at least 44×44. WCAG 2.2’s AA target minimum is 24×24 with exceptions, so the larger product targets deliberately exceed that floor. Preserve 320 CSS px reflow, zoom, visible focus, meaningful headings, and textual status changes; never announce every timer tick. WCAG’s contrast requirement for ordinary text is 4.5:1 and 3:1 for large text. [10](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) [11](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)

Use ordinary release/click behavior outside the timed answer pad. W3C permits essential down-event interactions in limited cases; a timing-sensitive pad needs its rationale documented and accessible activation tested. Do not treat every game control as exempt. Keyboard shortcuts must ignore text fields and repeated keydown, with equivalent visible controls. Timed competition may depend on an essential timer, but this does not justify timed menus, vanishing explanations, or excluding an untimed practice path. [12](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pointer-cancellation.html) [13](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/timing-adjustable.html)
Hooks and roadmap gates

Launch with intrinsic hooks: a remembered favorite field, a satisfying fact explanation, optional collection, and deliberate rematch. Add themed editorial packs after the question pool is deep enough. A later “Rivalry Card” can summarize a friend series without publicly exposing opponents’ identities. A later “Same Question, Your Time” asynchronous challenge can compare independently recorded attempts, but must be labelled differently from simultaneous live play and needs spoiler/replay controls.

Defer leaderboards, seasons, confidence stakes, tournaments, and collectible economies until content calibration, identity, anti-cheat, and sustainable operations exist. Never display invented popularity, expert percentages, learning scores, scarcity, or “people waiting.” A visit counter is a visit counter, not mastery. Offer finishing points instead of a streak penalty or a reward contingent on staying longer.

rows: New players can identify opponent type, start, answer, and explain result; record observed failures
Small phone, large text, keyboard, screen reader, reduced motion, both themes
Pending/accepted states, bot independence, source reveal timing, draw and interruption copy match engine
Source-backed explanation and non-repeating family coverage; saved review never leaks active answers
Cohort return and satisfaction alongside regret, accidental inputs, and disputed outcomes

design.text: Treat completion rate, voluntary second match, question-report rate, and later fact recall as separate measures. No numeric conversion or retention target is established by the cited studies. Start with observed private pilots; use small qualitative rounds to find comprehension failures, not to estimate population prevalence. Assign every issue an owner, severity, dependency, acceptance evidence, and status; a passed code test does not close a human usability issue.
Two critique loops

**Loop 1 — contract critique before release.** Independently inspect each state for an obvious main action, truthful copy, recoverable errors, contrast, keyboard behavior, source timing, and a bot label. Challenge the most attractive features: does a coin animation obscure correctness, does an identity badge imply expertise, and can pressing Back lose an accepted attempt? Record defects, implement bounded corrections, then recheck affected flows and settlement invariants.

**Loop 2 — field critique after those fixes.** Observe consenting testers across target geographies, phones, connection qualities, and accessibility settings completing bot play, a friend room, a close result, and an interruption. Ask them to explain what happened before explaining the rules yourself. Compare accidental selection, abandonment point, rule comprehension, and satisfaction with the previous build. Mark unresolved device or timing limitations explicitly; do not label a design “validated” because an advisor approved a screenshot.
Sources

1. Ryan, Rigby, and Przybylski. “The Motivational Pull of Video Games: A Self-Determination Theory Approach.” 2006. [Author-hosted paper](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2006_RyanRigbyPrzybylski_MandE.pdf).
2. Roediger and Karpicke. “Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention.” 2006. [Original abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16507066/).
3. Butler and Roediger. “Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing.” 2008. [Original abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18491500/).
4. Norman. *The Design of Everyday Things*, revised edition, 2013. [Author synopsis and contents](https://jnd.org/books/the-design-of-everyday-things-revised-and-expanded-edition/).

5. Krug. *Don’t Make Me Think, Revisited*, third edition, 2014. [Publisher overview and contents](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/don-t-make-me-think-revisited-a-common-sense-approach-to-web-usability/P200000000385/9780133597264).
6. Schell. *The Art of Game Design*, third edition, 2019. [Publisher featured-book description](https://www.routledge.com/about-us/crc-press).
